lead: Swapping moves whole processes between main memory and a designated area on secondary storage called swap space. It is used when RAM cannot hold all active processes, allowing the operating system to free memory for a newly ready process. Swapping is common in systems with limited RAM, such as low‑end servers, embedded devices, or during heavy load on a desktop when many applications are opened.
prereq: You need: Memory management strategies and address spaces.

blocks.text: Swap space is a reserved portion of the disk that the OS treats as an extension of RAM. It is created during system installation or by a system administrator. Each process that is swapped out has its entire address image written to one or more blocks in the swap area; the blocks need not be contiguous. The image includes code, data, stack and heap segments.

When a process is swapped in, the OS reads its image back into a free region of RAM. The process resumes execution as if it had never left memory. The whole operation is called a swap‑in (load) or swap‑out (store).

items: Swap space size is often chosen as a fraction or multiple of RAM, e.g., 1× to 2× RAM, but the optimal size depends on the workload and system configuration.

sections.h3: When swapping is invoked and its overhead

blocks.text: Swapping is invoked when the ready queue contains a process that cannot be placed in RAM because all frames are occupied. The OS selects a victim process, writes its image to swap, updates the process control block (PCB) to reflect the new location, and then loads the waiting process.

items: Check if a free frame exists.
If none, choose a victim process.
Write the victim’s entire memory image to swap (swap‑out).
Read the waiting process image from swap (swap‑in).
Update the PCB and schedule the process.

blocks.text: The overhead consists of disk I/O time, which is orders of magnitude slower than RAM access. A typical hard‑disk transfer rate of 100 MB/s translates to about 80 ms to move an 8 MB process image, while RAM access is in nanoseconds. Consequently, swapping can increase response time if used excessively.

sections.h3: Policy, difference from paging, and simple example

blocks.text: Swapping differs from paging in that paging moves fixed‑size pages, while swapping moves the whole process image. Paging allows a process to stay partially resident, reducing I/O, whereas swapping removes the process completely.

A simple policy taught in many syllabi is to swap out the longest idle process. The OS maintains a timestamp of the last CPU burst for each resident process. The one with the earliest timestamp is selected as the victim.

items: Advantage: easy to implement, no need for page‑level bookkeeping.
Disadvantage: large I/O cost, may evict a process that will be needed soon.

examples.question: RAM = 16 MB, swap space = 32 MB, processes P1‑P4 each need 8 MB. After loading P1 and P2, the scheduler wants to run P3. Using the longest‑idle policy, which process is swapped out and how much memory is freed?
steps: Step 1: Total RAM = 16 MB, each process = 8 MB, so two processes fit.
Step 2: P1 is loaded first, then P2. P1 has been idle longer than P2.
Step 3: The longest‑idle victim is P1.
Step 4: Swapping out P1 writes its 8 MB image to swap and frees 8 MB of RAM.
Step 5: P3 is loaded into the freed 8 MB region.
examples.answer: Process P1 is swapped out, freeing 8 MB of RAM.

traps: Assuming swapping always improves response time without accounting for the disk I/O delay.
Confusing swapping with paging and thinking that a swapped‑out process still occupies RAM frames.
Swapping the process that just used the CPU because it appears in the ready queue, ignoring the longest‑idle rule.
Using the size of swap space as a limit for how many processes can be resident, instead of RAM size.

quiz.q: What is the name of the disk area reserved for storing whole process images?
Explain why swapping can increase the overall execution time of a process.
quiz.a: Swapping requires writing the entire process image to disk and later reading it back. Disk I/O is orders of magnitude slower than RAM access, so the extra transfer time adds to the process’s execution time.

quiz.q: Given RAM = 24 MB and four processes each needing 10 MB, which process(s) must be swapped out before a fifth process of 10 MB can run, using the longest‑idle policy?
quiz.a: Only two processes can be resident in 24 MB RAM (20 MB used). To run a third (or fifth) 10 MB process, one of the resident processes must be swapped out. Using the longest‑idle policy, swap out the resident process that has been idle the longest, freeing 10 MB for the new process.

quiz.q: Calculate the swap‑out time for a 12 MB process if the disk transfer rate is 80 MB/s.
quiz.a: Swap‑out time = 12 MB ÷ 80 MB/s = 0.15 s (150 ms).

quiz.q: A system frequently swaps processes even though RAM usage is below 50 %. Identify two possible reasons for this behaviour.
quiz.a: 1) The OS may use a low‑priority swapping daemon to pre‑emptively move idle processes to swap and keep RAM free for bursty workloads. 2) Misconfiguration of the swap‑out policy (e.g., aggressive idle‑time threshold) can cause premature swapping.

quiz.q: True or false: After a process is swapped out, its page table entries remain valid in RAM.
quiz.a: False. The page table entries are marked invalid because the frames are no longer occupied.

beyond: Not for the exam. In modern cloud servers, swapping is often replaced by ballooning or live migration to avoid large I/O penalties. Research on fast non‑volatile memory (NVMe, Intel Optane) blurs the line between RAM and swap, enabling new hybrid memory managers. To explore current trends, search for "memory tiering" and "transparent huge pages" in Linux kernel documentation.
